title: Epistolarum Libri Decem
author: Aurelius Symmachus
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0271.stoa002.opp-lat4, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Postquam te jactatam comperi dolore consueto, omnis reliquarum sollicitudinum mearum sensus evannit. Na(??), ut ait Hippocrates : Praesentia hebe- tantur incommoda, si cui dolor major accesserit. Exspecto igitur, ut accepto de te indicio laetiore, in priores curas re verior. Caetera in hoc consternatione animi mei tanquam intempestiva praetereo, et tamen commonitorium junxi, quod velim redacta in tran- quillum sanitate consideres.
passages.english: After I learned that you were troubled by your usual pain, all feeling of my other anxieties vanished. For, as Hippocrates says: present discomforts are dulled if a greater pain comes upon someone. I am waiting, therefore, to return to my former cares once I have received happier news about you. Everything else I pass over in this distress of my mind as untimely; and yet I have attached a memorandum, which I would like you to consider once your health has been restored to calm.
passages.notes: "evannit" read as "evanuit"; "Na(??)" as "Nam"; "re verior" as "revertar" (the printed form is garbled; sense 'return' is clear). "in hoc consternatione" is ungrammatical as printed; read as "in hac consternatione". The Hippocratic saying corresponds to Aphorisms 2.46.

passages.original: Recte Caecilius comicus : Homo, inquit, homini deus est, si suum officium sciat. Hanc ego in te dixe- rim sententiam convenire, qui nostris negotiis curam vigilem praestitisti. Hinc in pectore memoria, laus in ore versatur.
passages.english: The comic poet Caecilius put it rightly: "Man," he says, "is a god to man, if he knows his duty." I would say that this maxim fits you, who have given watchful care to my affairs. Hence the memory [of it] dwells in my heart, and praise on my lips.
passages.notes: "dixe- rim" is a line-break split for "dixerim". "nostris negotiis" is taken as an authorial plural ("my affairs"); it could also mean "our affairs".

passages.original: Quod si mihi ullus honor testimonii publici affectan- dus foret; judicio tuo et similium contentus esse de- berem, vel fidicinis exemplo, qui indignatus consi- dentium turbam, sibi et musis cantum ciebat; vel secundum Heraclitum philosophum, qui summam laudis arbitrabatur placere uni, si esset optimus qui probaret. Quare esto securus patientiae nostrae, et congratulare mihi quod solus torqueo corda liven- tium, cum alii quibus statuae quoquo modo tributae sint, nihil habeant invidendum.
passages.english: But if I had to strive after any honour of public testimony, I ought to be content with your judgement and that of men like you, following either the example of the lyre-player who, scorning the crowd of those seated [to hear him], raised his song for himself and the Muses; or [the view] of the philosopher Heraclitus, who considered it the height of praise to please one man, provided he who approved was the best. Therefore be easy about my patience, and congratulate me that I alone torment the hearts of the envious, while others, to whom statues have been granted in whatever way, have nothing to be envied.
passages.notes: The saying about pleasing one man, if he is the best, is attributed to Heraclitus here; the ascription is the author's.
